scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet the smart pointer that you will use most. It owns a heap object, and it frees the object for you.

scenes.onScreen: "unique_ptr": numbered lines (1. A unique_ptr owns one heap object; 2. It deletes the object by itself; 3. It cannot be copied, only moved) and an analogy card: a house key with one owner: you can hand it over, but you cannot copy it
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A unique pointer owns one heap object. When the unique pointer dies, it deletes the object. You never write delete. This is RAII for heap memory. A unique pointer has one owner. You cannot copy it, but you can move it to a new owner. Think of a house key with one owner. You can hand it over, but you cannot copy it. Modern C plus plus advises you to avoid raw new and delete. Smart pointers do the work. Unique pointer is the first choice. It costs nothing extra. It is as fast as a raw pointer, and it deletes the object at the right time.
points: A unique_ptr owns one heap object
It deletes the object by itself
It cannot be copied, only moved

scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 2] The memory header holds the smart pointers. [HL 6] Make unique builds an int with the value five on the heap. The unique pointer p owns it. [HL 7] Star works as before. It reads five. [HL 8] We change it to eight. [HL 10] At the end of main, p dies and deletes the int. There is no delete in our code. [HL 6] Make unique builds the int on the heap, and the unique pointer owns it. [HL 7] The star works as with a raw pointer. We see five. [HL 8] We can change the value, as before. [HL 10] When main ends, the unique pointer dies, and the heap box is freed. We wrote no delete.

scenes.onScreen: the unique_ptr on the stack owns the int on the heap
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the arrow. P owns the int on the heap. There is only one owner. When p goes out of scope, it deletes the int. A raw pointer has no such duty. It only points. Notice the single owner. The key has one holder. If you hand the key to someone else, you no longer have it. This rule makes double delete impossible.

scenes.onScreen: moveown.cpp: std::move hands the object to another unique_ptr
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 7] A owns an int with the value five. [HL 8] Move hands the ownership to b. [HL 9] A is now empty. It equals nullptr, so the program prints one. [HL 10] B owns the int and reads five. When b dies, the int is deleted exactly once. [HL 8] The move function hands the object from a to b. After that, a is empty. [HL 9] A moved-from pointer equals nullptr, so the test prints one. [HL 10] The new owner b still sees the value five.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as moveown dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints one, and then five. Notice that a is empty, and b holds the value. Ownership moved, and nothing was copied.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A unique pointer owns one heap object. Two. It deletes the object when it dies. Three. It cannot be copied. Four. Use move to hand over the ownership. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A unique pointer owns one heap object.
It deletes the object when it dies.
Use move to hand over the ownership.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Copying a unique_ptr
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We copy a unique pointer. The compiler says use of deleted function. The copy is blocked on purpose. Two owners would delete the object twice. Use move to hand over the ownership. If two unique pointers owned one object, both would delete it. That is a crash. So the language does not allow a copy. When you want a new owner, say so with move. Then the old pointer becomes empty.

scenes.onScreen: A unique pointer never shares its umbrella. It is all about ownership.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

moveown.cpp: In function 'int main()':
moveown.cpp:7:25: error: use of deleted function 'std::unique_ptr<_Tp, _Dp>::unique_ptr(const std::unique_ptr<_Tp, _Dp>&) [with _Tp = int; _Dp = std::default_delete<int>]'
    7 |     unique_ptr<int> b = a;
      |                         ^
bug.why: Two unique pointers must never own the same object, or it would be deleted twice. The compiler blocks the copy. Use move.
